https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yr.text: Image source, Twitter/@ABDELAESPRIELLA Image caption, Hernando Forero Mosquera, aka "El ruso", is accused of leading a dissident rebel faction By Vanessa BuschschlÃ¼ter Latin America online editor Published 28 minutes ago A man suspected of leading a dissident faction of a left-wing rebel group has been killed in a military operation in central Colombia, officials say. The operation forms part of a crackdown on illegal armed groups ordered by Colombia's new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, who was sworn in on Friday. He said the killing by the security forces of Hernando Forero Mosquera and five other alleged members of armed groups on the weekend sent "a clear and powerful message to all bandits that there is nowhere for them to hide". During his campaign for the presidency, de la Espriella said he would target "narco-terrorism" relentlessly, including by launching air strikes. Image source, Colombian Presidency/Handout via REUTERS Image caption, Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in on Friday as Colombia's new president Military intelligence officers said that Forero led a group known as Frente 28, which is one of the many dissident factions to have sprung forth from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc). The Farc, Colombia's largest left-wing rebel group , signed a peace deal with the government in 2016 but some of its members did not agree to the terms of the deal and refused to lay down their arms. These dissidents groups, which are now mainly involved in cocaine trafficking and illegal mining, are among the main driving forces behind the resurgence in violence in the country . De la Espriella said he would take a radically different approach to defeating criminal groups in the country than his predecessor in office, Gustavo Petro. Petro, the first left-wing politician to be elected president of Colombia, advocated what he called a "total peace" strategy, which prioritised negotiation over confrontation. His attempts to negotiate with a number of armed groups, however, failed as members of the illegal organisations repeatedly broke ceasefires and walked away from the talks. De la Espriella's combative approach has been met with defiance by dissident rebel groups. On Saturday, just a day after the was sworn into office, two explosive devices went off. In Cauca province, a car bomb exploded at a tollbooth, injuring two security guards, and in Cesar province, a police officer was killed by explosives dropped from a drone. In a video uploaded to social media, de la Espriella praised the military for killing Forero, who was also known as "El ruso" (The Russian), and whom he described as an explosives expert. He added that three more alleged members of the dissident group had been killed in the military operation in a rural area in Meta province. The president also said that soldiers had killed two alleged members of another criminal group, the Gulf Clan, in a separate offensive in Antioquia province. De la Espriella has the backing of US President Donald Trump, who endorsed his candidacy. On Friday, the US state department said it planned to provide $1bn (Â£740m) in security assistance to de la Espriella's government. It also welcomed Colombia into the US-led group dubbed " Shield of the Americas " - an alliance of Western Hemisphere countries which have pledged to co-operate in their fight against drug trafficking gangs and transnational crime. Photograph: Luke Gartside/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Cornwall was one of the best places in the UK to view the solar eclipse. Photograph: Luke Gartside/The Guardian Solar eclipses ‘A magical eeriness’: Cornwall comes together for communal moment during solar eclipse People came from far and wide to witness phenomenon that has thrilled humans for thousands of years Steven Morris Cornwall Wed 12 Aug 2026 15.55 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 18.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At 6pm the beach and village began to empty, and those in the know headed up the hill towards the old granite coastguard station on the headland. “This is the best spot,” said Sennen Cove resident Lisa Redfern, who had built a pinhole camera for the eclipse out of an old Ryvita Thins box. As the moon began to hide the sun and Redfern – just about – got her makeshift device to work, she felt a little emotional. “I’d describe it as a magical eeriness,” she said. “Let’s face it, we may not see another one. We have to make the most of these moments.” It was certainly a wonderful communal moment. Redfern was part of a big group of friends and family who enjoyed a picnic (including Pringles and prosecco) on the headland. Matthew Robinson came armed with a colander and spent a frustrating few minutes getting the angle right. “The colander is a bit disappointing, but there’s a lovely atmosphere here.” 0:31 Iceland in complete darkness during total solar eclipse - video Another member of the group, seven-year-old Rina, did have the proper eclipse glasses. “It’s like someone has taken a bite out of a biscuit,” she said as the eclipse began. Strangers shared picnics, drinks and eclipse glasses, which had been very tricky to source in Cornwall . The wind picked up as the eclipse took hold and the temperature, which had reached the 30s during the day, plunged. Gulls stopped circling and landed on the surface of the water. A trio of choughs – Cornwall’s national bird – hopped around on the hillside, looking a little less graceful than usual. The swallows that had been whizzing around the thatched cottages rested for a while. Mary Bendall had positioned herself on a rock near the coastguard station with a complicated setup involving a filter over a scope that she uses to watch wildlife and her iPhone. She watched the total eclipse in 1999 with her daughter, who now works in physics, having been inspired by the experience. “I have just spoken to her – she’s in Spain. It’s cloudy there so we may be having the best of it,” Bendall said. View image in fullscreen Some set out to sea to see the eclipse. Photograph: Luke Gartside/The Guardian Across Cornwall, one of the best places in the UK to view the eclipse, towns, villages and pubs staged special events as people came from far and wide to drink in a phenomenon that has thrilled – and frightened – human beings for thousands of years In the harbour port of Falmouth, they clearly didn’t think the astronomical phenomenon was enough and an air display was arranged. One of the hotels also hosted an evening of sea shanties. Elsewhere, the playlist blaring from radios and pubs was predictable – Van Morrison’s Moondance and the Whole of the Moon by the Waterboys. Members of Kernow Astronomers were posted at the National Trust’s site Carnewas at Bedruthan, near Padstow, with telescopes fitted with filters to enable visitors to observe the eclipse safely. Inland, people had gathered on hilltops, near castles, close to one of Cornwall’s many standing stones. Carolyn Kennett, a Cornish expert in archaeoastronomy, said eclipses would almost certainly have been unexpected for ancient people and would have inspired awe, wonder and, perhaps, terror. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion She said: “An eclipse is a powerful spectacle, and for people without a modern scientific explanation, such an event would likely have carried profound meaning. View image in fullscreen A technical approach to the eclipse. Photograph: Luke Gartside/The Guardian “It is possible that witnessing an eclipse influenced the beliefs, stories, rituals or even choices of those who experienced one.” The Rev Karsten Wedgewood, priest in charge of St Just in Penwith, near Sennen, planned a picnic at a prehistoric funerary cairn, and a prayer based on psalm 8, known as the psalm for stargazers – “When I consider your heavens/the work of your fingers, / the moon and the stars …” At one point, one of the woes of modern life seemed destined to intervene when a pall of smoke from a wildfire near Land’s End airport threatened to dim the spectacle. A series of wildfires has been fought in Cornwall over the past few days but it did not affect the view from Sennen, at least. Coastguards and lifeguards had advised those intending to watch from kayaks or surfboards or take an eclipse sea dip to remember that it was going to turn a little colder and, of course, visibility would be poorer. A crew from the Cape Cornwall Pilot Gig Club put out to sea from Sennen harbour but returned before the darkness fell and fired up the barbecue instead. Surf photographer Jules River did paddle out on his board. “This is a kind of pilgrimage for me – it feels very soulful and healing to be here when this is happening.” There were good views to be had in the village as well as on the headland. Mother and daughter Lisa and Janet Grenfell, 53 and 79, plonked their camp chairs on the front and took it all in. “We remember the total eclipse in 1999 but it was cloudy. This is beautiful.” Jasmine Owen and Rory Smith arguably had the best seat in the house – a table overlooking the ocean where they tucked into fish and chips. What was better? The supper or the eclipse? Owen did not hesitate: “The chips are great, the eclipse amazing.” Explore more on these topics Solar eclipses Cornwall Space news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Europe solar eclipse: millions watch rare spectacle across Spain, UK and Iceland – as it happened WhatsApp ‘drops’, price hikes and queues: scramble for solar eclipse specs Great Britain braced to pay millions for backup electricity during solar eclipse ‘It’s going to be spectacular’: Millions flock to Spain seeking best view of total solar eclipse How to safely watch the solar eclipse Europe’s total solar eclipse: the best place to see it and how to view it safely ‘You’re hit with a slam of shadow’: Nasa’s air mission to capture rare eclipse data Where in the UK will get the best view of the solar eclipse? Photograph: supplied by the Ticehurst family View image in fullscreen Daniel Billings pled guilty to stabbing Molly Ticehurst, a 28-year-old childcare educator, to death in April 2024. Photograph: supplied by the Ticehurst family Australia news Man who murdered Molly Ticehurst unlikely to face life in jail, court hears Justice Natalie Adams says she is troubled by expert evidence about rape allegations in slain woman’s police statement Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian Associated Press Mon 31 Aug 2026 03.11 EDT First published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Molly Ticehurst’s ex-boyfriend is unlikely to face a life sentence for her domestic violence murder, a crime which galvanised a national movement against gendered abuse. Ticehurst, a 28-year-old childcare educator, was found dead in her home at Forbes, in the New South Wales central-west, in the early hours of 22 April 2024. Her former boyfriend Daniel Billings broke into her bedroom and stabbed her 15 times in a ferocious attack that lasted less than a minute. Billings had been charged with several counts of raping Ticehurst and a string of domestic violence offences just over two weeks before the killing, but he was freed on bail by a local court registrar the next day. Ticehurst’s death became a flashpoint in the nation’s fight against domestic violence and led to legal changes in NSW, including tighter bail laws. Billings, 31, who has pleaded guilty to murder, is will face court in Orange for a two-day sentence hearing from Thursday. During a mention in the NSW supreme court on Monday, Adams raised the issue of a life sentence, although she noted she did not expect it to be requested. Crown submissions before the court do not seek a life term, but they argue Billings should not get any discount on his sentence because his level of culpability is “extreme”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Adams said there would probably be mitigating factors to consider when sentencing Billings, as there were in almost all cases. “It’s difficult to identify what’s [legally] unique about this case,” she said. But the judge said she was troubled with how to deal with expert evidence about Ticehurst’s police statement that she was repeatedly raped by Billings. The sexual assault charges were dropped when Billings pleaded guilty to murder in November 2025 after 18 months of legal negotiations. Billings always denied raping Ticehurst and developed a dark obsession with clearing his name in the lead-up to the murder. “If I’m going to do the time, I may as well do the crime,” he said in a conversation with a friend soon before the murder, according to a statement of agreed facts before the court. Adams said she could not ignore the rape allegations, despite the charges being dropped, when it came to sentencing Billings for murder. “It was him seeing the police facts that set him to spiral,” the judge said. Acting out of spite over the allegations could push his crime into another serious category, she said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “The sense of grievance about a perceived false allegation, there’s no getting around that,” Adams said. “Whether it’s almost a public-justice type murder or domestic-violence type murder.” Adams said it was possible all the elements to satisfy the legal definition of sexual assault were in Ticehurst’s account to police. Changes to consent laws in NSW, which included affirmative language in the legislation, meant it was a crime where both parties “feel they’re telling the truth”. “The only witness who could have told us is dead,” the judge said. Billings, who has been in custody in the supermax wing of Goulburn jail since he was charged, will face court in person. He will hear victim impact statements from the Ticehurst family, along with expert evidence about his mental state at the time of the murder. A series of videos he made before and after the murder are also expected to be played to court. Ticehurst’s death became a flashpoint in the nation’s fight against domestic violence and led to legal changes in NSW, including tighter bail laws. Adams has indicated she will sentence Billings later in September. https://www.dw.com/en/saudi-arabia-houth.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MthS Saudi Arabia has not commented on the threat mentioned in the warnings sent overnight Image: REUTERS Advertisement Yemen-based Houthi rebels said they targeted "sensitive sites" in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and oil facilities in the port city of Yanbu on Saturday. A statement posted to Telegram from the Iran-backed group came hours after firefighters extinguished a blaze at a fuel depot near King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital. Earlier, residents reported hearing explosions in the vicinity, following overnight warnings by Saudi authorities of a "hostile aerial threat." The Saudi government has yet to confirm the blasts. What did the Houthis say? Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the rebels had "carried out two successful military operations using a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones." Saree continued: "The first targeted sensitive sites in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu." He said the attacks were in retaliation for recent Saudi attacks on the Yemeni capital Sana'a. The fresh violence comes just days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting the Holy city of Mecca, which the Iran-backed militants denied as a "worn-out lie." An overnight air raid alert was issued by Saudi authorities, the first since fighting in neighbouring Yemen intensified this month Image: REUTERS What do we know about the airport strike? AFP journalists then reported hearing two explosions before the Saudi civil defence agency lifted the alert half an hour later. "The area is under a hostile aerial threat," a message sent to Riyadh residents warned overnight, urging them to stay indoors, AFP news agency reported. News agency Reuters later published video and photos of a large plume of black smoke rising from an area near a highway to the airport. Saudi authorities also reported intercepting incoming Houthi missiles and drones. Saudi Arabia short of options against Iran-aligned Houthis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Tracking website FlightRadar24 reported "major problems" at the King Khalid International Airport, listing it under its maximum disruption index. Unravelling security situation The latest developments come amid an escalation between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government in Yemen that is supported by Saudi Arabia. A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia fell apart in July after the rebels allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace. As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia. The group has reported dozens of Saudi strikes since its recent offensive to secure control over the coastal areas near the Red Sea's Bab al-Mandeb Strait — a vital global shipping route — from government hands. https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text: European states clarify position on trade with Israeli settlements Several European governments have said they would restrict trade with illegal Israeli settlements only through a collective EU decision, following confusion over a joint statement on Israel’s actions in the occupied West Bank. Sweden, Denmark and Finland currently have no plans to introduce unilateral measures. The Danish embassy told Haaretz that Copenhagen supported EU-wide restrictions, while Poland’s ambassador said Warsaw could consider imposing its own sanctions. Britain, France and Canada are separately pursuing national bans on trade in settlement goods. The UK has also widened its sanctions framework to include individuals and companies involved in building, expanding or financing settlements. The measures could cover those participating in Israel’s E1 settlement project in the occupied West Bank.

https://brobible.com/culture/article/rep.text: Culture Former US Army Sniper Claims Troops Got Into Battle With ‘Reptilian Beings’ At Area 51 Base; Soldier’s Death Covered Up #Area 51 Follow Us Add as preferred source on Google 0 Comments Add as preferred source on Google 0 Comments by Eric Italiano October 16, 2026 1:39 pm iStockphoto A former Army sniper claimed a JSOC member told him U.S. troops killed three reptilian-looking creatures at an underground facility near Area 51 A former Army sniper claims that a drunk special operations soldier told him about a battle with “mildly reptilian” creatures that occurred at an underground base near Area 51. Nick Betts, co-host of the Liberty Risk podcast, says he was in Poland filming a documentary about the war in Ukraine when a man he described as a member of Joint Special Operations Command shared a story about a battle with reptilian creatures at Area 51 . While the operations soldier was drunk at the time, Betts said he was not sloppy. A former Army sniper claimed a JSOC member told him U.S. troops killed three reptilian-looking creatures at an underground facility near Area 51 According to Betts , the unit was pulled from Fort Bragg and flown to Area 51, where the soldiers were reportedly briefed and issued unfamiliar energy weapons that fired blasts instead of bullets. From there, they were allegedly taken by Black Hawk helicopter to the mouth of a long tunnel leading into the underground complex. Betts says the mission began when the facility stopped sending its routine radio check-ins, and a quick-reaction force sent to investigate never came back. He didn’t say whether his source knew what happened to those soldiers or whether they were still missing. Once inside, the source claimed, a team of about six soldiers worked their way through the tunnels and ran into the first reptilian creature, which was reportedly armed with the same kind of weapon the team had been issued. Inside, a serviceman was killed by a weapon fired from a creature that walked on two legs, looked “mildly reptilian,” and had fingers. “As they’re coming around on this outside, the outside left guy gets f—— hosed with one of the guns that they’re using, as straight to the chest and f—— dies.” “They said that they f—— shot this creature that was bipedal, mildly reptilian-looking but had fingers and was using this weapon system,” Betts said. Betts didn’t name the soldier or the unit, and a second special forces member who might have backed up the story wasn’t in the room when it was told. The team killed all three beings, and the soldier’s death was allegedly covered up. Despite how fantastical the story sounds, Betts said he believed them, though, given how serious they were about him not repeating what they told him. “I would have chalked it up to the wine if it wasn’t for being choke slammed up against a f—— wall in the morning at 6am,” Betts recalled. Betts’ anecdote is just the latest instance of a story about aliens/reptilians crossing paths with the military.
